canberra.title: Brad Pitt, a furry friend and a battle against the wilderness prove to be a winning formula
canberra.snippet: While Brad Pitt has always been a Hollywood heavyweight, starring in some of the most popular movies of all time including Fight Club, Se...
canberra.content:
Brad Pitt and Uber the German shepherd star in a new survival thriller, Heart of the Beast. Photo: Paramount Pictures.

While Brad Pitt has always been a Hollywood heavyweight, starring in some of the most popular movies of all time including Fight Club, Se7en and the Oceans’ movies, his most recent run of films might be his best.

Since 2019, the icon has won a Best Supporting Actor Oscar for Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, been a charismatic action hero in Bullet Train, driven the world’s fastest cars in F1: The Movie and most recently survived the wilderness in Heart of the Beast.

Heart of the Beast is the latest example of Brad Pitt playing whatever role he wants because he’s Brad Pitt.

While it might not be the best film in his four-decade-long catalogue of movies, it is one of his more interesting and definitely a new string in the bow for the actor who has done almost everything.

Heart of the Beast follows Retired Special Forces Command Sergeant Major James Belmont and his service dog Odin. The pair regularly fly a seaplane over the Alaskan wilderness as they keep to themselves instead of interacting with the rest of the world.

While on a flyover, James suffers a heart attack mid-flight, resulting in the plane crashing into a lake in the Alaskan wilderness.

The remainder of the movie follows James and Odin’s trek back to civilisation and the different challenges the wild frontier throws their way.

Due to small casts, survival movies like Heart of the Beast require a strong lead actor to keep audiences engaged with the story. Fortunately and unsurprisingly, Pitt delivers that here.

His characterisation of Belmont is fantastic. He’s clearly a troubled soul, consistently reliving the horrors of his time serving in the military. It’s demonstrated from the get-go.

These details are important because they give the audience an insight into who he is and why they should care for him. So, come the crash at the end of the first act, there is already some heavy weight being felt.

Add in a loyal canine companion and the movie has all the pieces it needs for an emotional roller coaster.

Another win for Heart of the Beast is its location. While survival movies aren’t a new genre by any stretch, the Alaskan wilderness and its extremes of light and dark are unique.

It means the scenery always pops and, in glorious 4K resolution, it at times feels like a nature documentary.

There are some hard-to-watch scenes here, especially an interaction involving a bear. It’s not at the level of Leonardo DiCaprio in The Revenant, but it’s still difficult nonetheless.

It looked very gruelling to film and it’s a testament to director David Ayer and his crew that they were able to pull it together.

The only real issues are to do with the film’s pacing. This is solely because of James’ flashback to his time in the military. The film isn’t long by any means, clocking in at around 100 minutes, but when the flashbacks do occur, it feels like the momentum of James’ survival is lost.

The flashbacks serve the narrative and don’t pull the audience out of the immersion, but they are stark in contrast.

Heart of the Beast is ultimately a winner. While not quite the heights of Cast Away in terms of survival films, it’s definitely a welcome addition to Brad Pitt’s incredible filmography.

Heart of the Beast is now showing in cinemas across the country.

canberra.title: How much are Canberra petrol retailers making? Fuel inquiry to examine margins and price gap
canberra.snippet: Why Canberra motorists pay more for petrol than drivers just across the border and how much retailers are making from each litre. These a...
canberra.content:
4 October 2026

Start the conversation

The ACT Government has finally launched an enquiry into Canberra’s petrol prices after they continued to soar following the removal of excise duty. Photo: File.

Why Canberra motorists pay more for petrol than drivers just across the border and how much retailers are making from each litre. These are a few questions that will be put under the microscope as the ACT’s latest fuel inquiry gets underway.

The Legislative Assembly’s Standing Committee on Economics, Industry and Recreation will examine current retail margins, terminal-gate prices and the difference between fuel prices in Canberra and surrounding markets.

It will also look back at the problems identified by the Independent Competition and Regulatory Commission (ICRC) and a previous Assembly inquiry in 2019 to determine whether they still exist seven years later.

At the heart of the inquiry will be another question: did the changes made after the last investigation actually work?

Measures introduced following the 2019 inquiry included greater monitoring of fuel prices and competition and the extension of the NSW FuelCheck scheme to the ACT.

The committee will examine whether those measures have been effective and whether existing systems are good enough to detect and respond when Canberra fuel prices move unusually.

That will include examining the role of the ICRC and whether existing fair trading laws and other regulatory arrangements are doing enough.

The inquiry comes as the latest Australian Competition and Consumer Commission data again put Canberra fuel prices in the spotlight.

On 16 September, Canberra recorded the highest average petrol price of Australia’s eight capital cities, after prices jumped 17.3 cents a litre in a week, the largest increase of any capital.

The latest investigation follows a push by Opposition Leader Mark Parton during the recent Assembly sitting week, which won support from Labor, Greens and independent MLAs.

It is not the first attempt to understand why Canberra motorists can pay more.

A select committee established in 2019 examined the structure of the ACT fuel market, differences between Canberra and surrounding communities and possible regulatory responses.

Its five recommendations included closer monitoring of fuel prices and competition, attracting more independent operators, introducing real-time price monitoring and examining service station operating costs.

Speaking at the assembly, Planning and Sustainable Development Minister Chris Steel said Labor supported another committee inquiry but rejected suggestions the government had failed to act on those recommendations.

He said all ACT fuel retailers now participated in NSW FuelCheck, while the Treasury continued to monitor prices using FuelCheck, ACCC data and other market information.

But Mr Steel said previous investigations had identified competition within Canberra’s fuel market as an underlying issue.

Earlier ICRC findings linked Canberra’s higher average retail margins to a more concentrated market, fewer aggressive discount retailers and a greater proportion of retailers operating premium business models.

The new inquiry will now test whether those conditions remain and whether seven years of monitoring and other changes have made a meaningful difference.

The committee is chaired by Labor MLA Taimus Werner-Gibbings, with independent MLA Fiona Carrick as deputy chair. Liberal MLA Elizabeth Lee, independent MLA Thomas Emerson and Greens MLA Rebecca Vassarotti are also members.

Submissions are now open until 5 pm, 16 November, giving motorists, retailers, industry groups and other interested parties an opportunity to tell the committee what they believe is driving Canberra’s fuel prices.

canberra.title: I escaped to the country dreaming of life surrounded by animals. I wasn’t prepared for reality
canberra.snippet: We moved to the country over 10 years ago, drawn by a combination of affordable property prices, peace and quiet, and wide open spaces. A...
canberra.content:
Doris (Day) and Julie (Andrews) came to us from a Wagga-based animal rescue organisation, having been born in transit on a livestock transport truck. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

We moved to the country over 10 years ago, drawn by a combination of affordable property prices, peace and quiet, and wide open spaces.

At least, those are the factors I nodded along with as my husband justified our decision.

For me? It was always about the animals.

How many animals can I surround myself with? Which paddock will be for the llamas? Where shall I put my wildlife rehabilitation centre? Where will the macropod nursery go?

I’ll start small though, I thought. What first? Miniature cows, dwarf goats or micro-pigs?

I’m joking, obviously. While I would never turn away a tiny cow (a heartbreaking image), I love animals of all shapes, sizes and species.

One should never acquire an animal based on its ability to fit in a teacup.

Ten years ago, I naively thought my rural escape would be entirely idyllic. Sunrises spent feeding the farmyard at a yonder big red barn, nursing orphaned piglets back to full health, baking pies with woodland creatures – that sort of thing.

But I’m no longer an ignorant city slicker. I’ve outgrown my initial overenthusiasm (and any lingering obsession with diminutive animals) and – I think – found the sweet spot between animal lover and animal hoarder.

I’ve taken on poddy lambs who have emerged – unplanned and unwanted – from transport vehicles and into the arms of already overrun rescue organisations.

Our chook enclosure is home to a never-ending stream of rehomed middle-aged ladies.

We even have a resident male kangaroo. Having apparently been excommunicated by his mob, this curious squatter has called our backyard home for almost two years.

We did have a miniature bat for a while – but that was a Christmas tree related accident.

Poddy lambs have proved to be one of my most rewarding responsibilities.

Bird rescues are frequent, as are inventive new methods. This rosella is wearing my beanie.

Our resident kangaroo is a little too at home here.

Sometimes, calls for help come from inside the house - like the lizards I occasionally find living under our lounge.

If you're going to rescue a bird, do it dressed in Disney.

The only mini animals we've actually hosted.

Mini animals can prove big troublemakers.

What's better than a miniature horse? A baby miniature horse.

While to some degree I’ve been able to realise my dream of surrounding myself with animal sidekicks, what I wasn’t expecting was the flip side of that coin.

Surrounding yourself with animals comes with no shortage of chaos and, sadly, the inevitability of seeing them suffer, particularly when it comes to wildlife.

I won’t torture you with detail, but suffice to say I’ve experienced my fair share of incidents.

Many are stressful episodes which eventually morph into lighthearted memories. Like the lengths I went to reaching an injured kookaburra I’d seen hit by a car and flung, inconveniently, to the far side of a barbed-wire fence.

I stopped en route home to perform an impressive contortionist act for two confused kids in the backseat, only to find an extremely ungrateful bird resistant to my helpful hands.

Like a modern MacGyver, I used the only item in my boot – an empty canvas shopping bag – to keep its wings safe, and drove home with a disembodied abusive avian head snapping at me furiously. This is also the story of how my four-year-old learnt her first curse words.

Of course, many incidents aren’t funny at all – just heartbreaking.

Like the hours I’ve spent standing beside immobile kangaroos, trying to offer support without adding stress, helplessly assuring them that it’ll be over soon – one way or another.

Sometimes they survive and become stories to tell. Sometimes they don’t and we solemnly move on.

I certainly haven’t become immune to these gut-wrenching moments. I still shed my fair share of tears. But I have become a little more hardened – and a lot more practical.

I may not have realised my most overzealous animal whisperer dreams, but all rural residents – and road users – still have plenty of opportunities (and a responsibility) to care for animals in our day-to-day lives.

We don’t need a purpose-built rehab centre. We just do what we can.

I now have several animal welfare groups saved in my phone. Oh, and I always keep a towel in the boot. So never again will a furious kookaburra suffer the indignity of travelling in a Woolies bag.

canberra.title: WATCH: Cleanup begins after tornado hits Ulladulla
canberra.snippet: The South Coast community of Ulladulla has begun the cleanup today after a small tornado hit the centre of town on Saturday, 3 October. T...
canberra.content:
4 October 2026

Start the conversation

SES volunteers work to repair a roof in Ulladulla. Photo: SES.

The South Coast community of Ulladulla has begun the cleanup today after a small tornado hit the centre of town on Saturday, 3 October.

The Bureau of Meteorology recorded a maximum wind gust of 98 km/h in Ulladulla but a tornado can produce much stronger, highly localised winds than would have registered at the weather station.

Jack Ireland was travelling through from Adelaide to Sydney and randomly stopped in Ulladulla, capturing some of the mayhem on his phone.

“We were just having a peaceful coffee then out of nowhere this storm rolls in,” he said.

The really intense part appears to have lasted only a few minutes, but was extremely violent. One café owner described everything being swept away in about 30 seconds and there were reports of boats in the harbour being lifted from their moorings.

There was damage to roofs, roof tiles and skylights, as well as numerous fallen trees and powerlines.

The SES had received 34 calls for assistance in the Ulladulla area, with more expected as people assessed damage.

“Please be patient with us,” a spokesperson said yesterday.

“Thank you to our fellow units who answered the call to help – today Nowra and Batemans Bay, tomorrow St Georges Basin and Sutton. We are expecting better weather tomorrow and completion of remaining tasks.”

The tornado wasn’t an isolated weather event. The broader system produced damaging winds, large hail and heavy rainfall across NSW, with severe thunderstorm warnings extending into the Illawarra, Sydney and other parts of the state.

Original Article published by Kim Treasure on About Regional.

canberra.title: Take a walk on the wild side to check out Canberra Reptile Zoo’s new inhabitants
canberra.snippet: Some of the ACT’s most vulnerable creatures have a new home, with the Canberra Reptile Zoo unveiling a permanent enclosure. Launche...
canberra.content:
4 October 2026

Start the conversation

Canberra Reptile Zoo founder Peter Child has unveiled a new exhibition which draws attention to some of the region’s most vulnerable creatures, including Rosenberg’s monitors. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

Some of the ACT’s most vulnerable creatures have a new home, with the Canberra Reptile Zoo unveiling a permanent enclosure.

Launched by ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr, the new display is known as The Wild Side of Canberra, which highlights the different levels of vulnerability facing four different reptile and amphibian species living in the ACT.

Two of the new inhabitants, the grassland earless dragons and corroboree frogs, have been gifted to the zoo following conservation efforts by the ACT to raise the numbers of the respective species.

The donated animals are now past the stage where they can breed, but their display at the zoo educates visitors about the challenges they face.

Other new inhabitants are the Rosenberg monitors, which are becoming scarce around the ACT and the green and golden bell frogs.

Canberra Reptile Zoo founder Peter Child said it was an honour to be given permission by the ACT Government to home the vulnerable animals.

“The new exhibit that we’ve got here at the Canberra Reptile Zoo is something that we’re really proud of and we are really privileged to have,” he said.

“From time to time, we run temporary displays with some endangered species, but the ACT government has very generously offered us the ability to take some of the ex-breeding animals that are used in their conservation programs.

“These animals in The Wild Side of Canberra are very important to the ACT and by having them in these new enclosures, we can demonstrate just how vital these creatures are to our ecosystems and how we can prevent losing them.”

Green and golden bell frog (Litoria aurea). Photos: Jarryd Rowley.

Canberra grassland earless dragon (Tympanocryptis lineata).

Northern corroboree frog (Gyak).

Rosenberg's monitor (Wirria).

While not every animal featured in the new exhibit is endangered, most are seeing significantly lower numbers in the ACT than in the past or in other places across the country.

Mr Child said the new exhibit contextualised how and why the animals were vulnerable.

“What people need to recognise is, and let’s take the green and golden bell tree frog for example, they are completely extinct in the ACT,” he said.

“Since the 1980s, they haven’t found them anywhere in the wild here, but they are still around Newcastle, Sydney and some of the coastal regions.

“Another is the Rosenberg monitor. They are found quite abundantly in Western Australia and South Australia, but there is only one recognised colony left here.

“This new exhibition is about bringing attention to the issues some of these species are having.”

Mr Child said the Canberra Reptile Zoo was all about supporting vulnerable animals and encouraged visitors to support the zoo’s efforts.

“We are a not-for-profit here and everything we do goes to supporting the animals,” Mr Child said.

“We have worked with the United Ngunnawal Elders Council to best understand and look after these animals.

“We want to tell the stories of these animals and showcase them and the best way to do that is to come visit and see what we have going on.”

The Canberra Reptile Zoo is located on O’Hanlon Place in Nicholls and is open 10 am to 5 pm, seven days a week.

australia.title: No bail for P-plater over Newcastle crash that left five-year-old in induced coma and injured nine other NRL fans
australia.snippet: Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, appears in court on dangerous driving offences after car struck Knights supporters lining streets to fa...
australia.content:
A driver whose car careered into a crowd of Newcastle Knights supporters – leaving children as young as five injured – will be kept in custody as the community rallies to support those hospitalised after the crash.

Ten people were left injured after a car allegedly driven by 18-year-old P-plater Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe careered into the crowd near a major roundabout on Saturday morning.

Six people remain at the John Hunter hospital with injuries caused by the collision, according to the Hunter New England Local Health District chief executive, Tracey McCosker. Two are in a serious condition, while four are stable.

They include a five-year-old girl who had been placed into an induced coma with critical injuries, although her condition has stabilised.

Samarasinghe was taken to hospital for mandatory testing and subsequently charged with nine offences, including dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving and causing bodily harm by misconduct.

He did not make any application for release during a brief court appearance on Sunday, and he was formally refused bail. The judge also endorsed a warrant for a health assessment.

The bail court was told the most serious offence of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm carried a maximum jail term of seven years.

He will next appear at the Newcastle local court on 15 October.

Chris Clancy was among those injured in the crash, after joining thousands of Newcastle Knights fans to lined the streets to farewell their team as the players travelled to Sydney for the grand final.

“We’re there at the roundabout having fun – cars going past, beeping their horns, people waving,” Clancy said.

“The next thing, this car stops [at] the roundabout and then he just floored it on the wet ground, lost it.

“It happened in seconds, but when you stand there, seeing the car coming at you, I honestly thought I was going to die. It just felt like slow motion.”

Clancy suffered small fractures in his ribs and spine, a broken collarbone, and small fractures in his foot.

Investigators did not believe the incident was deliberate but declined to comment on reports the vehicle was being driven erratically before the crash.

Multiple fundraisers have been established for the victims of the incident, including one for the five-year-old girl and another for Wallsend grandfather Dave Martin.

Martin was injured after being struck by the car while trying to protect his two young granddaughters, sustaining multiple fractures in both legs and undergoing a lengthy surgery.

He was known in Wallsend for his love of the Knights, often decorating his barber shop on Nelson Street with team paraphernalia.

The Knights’ chief executive, Peter Parr, expressed deep concern for those affected by the crash.

“Newcastle is a strong community,” he said.

“We have seen that strength throughout this week, and today we need to draw on it again with compassion, care and support for those who need it most.”

australia.title: Chalmers says global economic turmoil will drive budget cuts, but Australia should avoid recession
australia.snippet: Treasurer says ‘very substantial and intensifying pressure’ on federal budget as he points finger at private sector for driving up inflat...
australia.content:
Jim Chalmers has warned of “very substantial and intensifying” economic pressures on the horizon but insists he’s not planning for a recession, as he prepares to find new ways to cut the budget ahead of its mid-year update.

The treasurer on Sunday called on critics of government spending to name the services that should be cut, as he points the finger at the private sector for driving up inflation in Australia amid the protracted conflict in the Middle East.

Chalmers said the US-led eight-month war against Iran, which has severely curtailed global oil supplies from the region, has been “disastrous” for cost-of-living pressures.

He also said there was “very substantial and intensifying pressure” on the federal budget.

“No serious observer of what’s going on right now would conclude anything other than [that],” he told ABC’s Insiders. “The longer this thing drags out, the bigger the impact on the global economy and on the Australian economy, whether it’s … on inflation or downward pressure on growth.

“We’re not anticipating [a recession] here in Australia, but certainly it is weighing on global growth, and we’re not immune from that.”

Inflation has jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%, while the Reserve Bank lifted its key interest rate to 4.6%, the highest figure since 2011.

Chalmers said the government was working on finding further savings to the budget in the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook, due in December, after cuts of $44.9bn over four years were identified in the May budget.

The treasurer said cuts to government spending weren’t the only factor driving up inflation in the economy, and cutting larger sums would impact essential services.

“If people don’t want us to strengthen Medicare, for example, or cut income taxes, or provide cost-of-living relief in other ways, then they should nominate where that should be cut,” he said on Sunday.

Beyond the war’s impact on driving up prices in Australia, Chalmers said the private sector was partly to blame.

“For every $5 of demand in our economy, $1 is public, $4 is private,” he said.

“Budget settings are not the primary driver of prices in our economy. There’s a whole bunch of other things going on.”

But the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, said Chalmers should be sacked, claiming his decisions have increased inflation to generate tax windfalls.

“He’s actively stoked inflation, and he’s fundamentally undermined the success of this country, and now he’s announced today he’s on a sort of Argo-style salvation trip for investment, because he’s created a problem of sovereign risk,” he told News24.

The assistant science and digital technology minister, Andrew Charlton, said the consequences of having a recession, which would ease inflation, would be devastating.

“If you have a recession, you throw hundreds of thousands of people on to the unemployment queues, and that pulls a huge amount of demand out of the economy,” he told News24.

“It’s pretty easy to have low interest rates and low inflation if your economy goes through a recession.

“As a Labor government, that is a big priority for us to make sure that we don’t go into a recession that drives a lot of people into unemployment.”

Chalmers will travel to Japan for meetings with business leaders and the country’s finance minister, in an effort to boost investment and improve fuel security.

australia.title: Flydubai co-pilot’s time in Australia being investigated by security agencies after alleged cockpit attack
australia.snippet: Police confirm investigation into period the man reportedly spent in Australia before alleged attempted terrorist attack Get our breaking...
australia.content:
Australian security agencies have launched an investigation after it emerged that the flydubai co-pilot who allegedly tried to hijack an Israel-bound flight spent about two years in the country as a student.

Disaster was narrowly averted on Wednesday when passengers and crew intervened to stop the co-pilot’s attempt to take control of the flydubai flight to Tel Aviv, which had 182 people onboard and plunged 16,625 feet (5,067 metres) in just over 30 seconds.

The United ⁠Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general has said the co-pilot had used a crash axe in the attempted “terrorist attack”, in which the pilot was stabbed mid-air. Numerous media outlets have named the co-pilot as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national.

A source familiar with the case, but not authorised to speak publicly, said the man was granted an Australian student visa in 2014, before arriving in the country to commence a university course the following year.

He left Australia in 2017, and his visa was cancelled in 2019 after authorities confirmed he was no longer enrolled in the course, the source said.

The Australian federal police (AFP) on Sunday said multiple agencies – including the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (Asio) – were probing the man’s connections to the country.

“The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team (VIC JCTT), comprising the AFP, Victoria Police and ASIO, can confirm it is investigating the man’s links to Australia,” an AFP spokesperson said.

“An update will be provided at an appropriate time.”

US media outlets, including CNN, reported that a now-deleted LinkedIn profile said al-Hammami had studied engineering at an Australian university. Guardian Australia has not verified which university the co-pilot attended.

It came after a British university, Buckinghamshire New University, said a student named Hamam al-Hammami had “previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management” at the institution. It added: “He did not undertake any pilot training at the university.”

A flydubai spokesperson on Saturday said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still ‌under investigation and the airline was not in a position to comment further.

The airline’s flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv have been suspended until further notice after the attack. The Omani co-pilot and the flight’s Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, were taken to the UAE, as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.

The Wall Street Journal has reported that the co-pilot had been barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views. He was then moved to an administrative job at Oman Air, according to the official, before being hired by the UAE-based budget airline flydubai.

australia.title: Five-year-old girl in a coma and P-plater charged after car hits crowd of NRL fans in Newcastle
australia.snippet: Man charged with nine offences after vehicle struck Knights fans attending grand final farewell, leaving 10 injured including three child...
australia.content:
Ten people have been injured, one critically, after a car crashed into a crowd of people in Newcastle waiting to farewell the Knights team bus before the NRL grand final.

New South Wales police said a five-year-old girl remained in a critical but stable condition in an induced coma after the crash on Saturday morning.

Initially a 67-year-old man was also in a critical. The man is now in a serious but stable condition.

John Hunter hospital provided an update to Australian Associated Press on Saturday night confirming five other patients were in a stable condition and three others had been discharged.

The injured were treated on the scene by NSW ambulance paramedics, before being taken to hospital.

Police said the P-plate driver was an 18-year-old man who was arrested at the scene and taken to hospital for mandatory testing and subsequently charged with nine offences including dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving and causing bodily harm by misconduct.

He was refused bail to appear in court on Sunday.

Assistant Commissioner Dave Waddell said two other people allegedly in the car were escorted from the crash scene after the crowd turned on them.

Police did not believe the incident was deliberate but declined to comment on reports the vehicle was allegedly being driven erratically before the accident.

“I’ll let the investigators from the crash investigation unit deal with that,” Waddell told reporters.

The police minister, Yasmin Catley, said so many lives had been affected by a split-second decision, as she urged other drivers to take care over the NSW long weekend.

“We have already started Saturday morning with this devastation,” she said.

“Nobody can comprehend what has happened with this terrible tragedy.”

The roads minister, Jenny Aitchison, said the incident could have been worse, with more than 1,000 people gathered in the area where it occurred.

Emergency services were called to Newcastle Link Road at the Transfield Drive roundabout in Wallsend about 9.30am on Saturday after reports a vehicle struck multiple people in a crowd.

“Several people have been injured and are currently receiving treatment at the scene,” police said.

“Police have commenced an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident, with initial inquiries indicating it is not believed to be terror related.”

Gavin Morris, the mayor of Newcastle, told the ABC that the driver, who he said was a Knights fan, lost control while revving his car shortly before the team arrived.

“I’ve spoken to the authorities, a number of which, and look, first of all, it is under investigation, and the young driver is now with police, so it appears that he was revving the car in some form. He was excited. He was a supporter. He was, you know, a fan,” Morris said.

“It appears that he’s lost control of the car, and he’s gone … sideways into the crowd.”

Footage posted on social media appeared to show a car being driven quickly around a roundabout shortly before the crash.

Other images showed it had careened off the road soon afterwards.

A witness to the incident, Dylan Prior, told ABC News that the car was “revving a bit” before it ran into a group of people.

“I saw some young kids go flying, and people running to help the victims,” he said.

“Everyone was yelling and hysterical, yelling at the driver.

“They were screaming for help.”

The Newcastle Link Road was closed in both directions, leading to the diversion of the Knights grand final procession.

The club confirmed in an Instagram post that it had changed its route, apologising to fans who may have missed farewelling the team but saying “public safety is our priority”.

Police appealed for fans to leave the area.

“Police acknowledge many loyal supporters may have missed the opportunity to see the team and show their support.

“Members of the public are asked to safely disperse from the area and keep roadways clear to assist emergency services and traffic management efforts.

“Police thank the community for their patience, cooperation and assistance.”

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, said his thoughts were with the families and friends of those injured.

“It’s heartbreaking to see fans who were sending off their grand final team involved in such a terrible incident,” he said. “We’ve seen how this grand final has brought Newcastle together, and I hope the whole community remains united as we continue to respond.”

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said he had spoken with Minns and offered the federal government’s support.

“My thoughts are with everyone injured or involved in the horrible incident this morning in Newcastle,” Albanese said in a statement. “I want to acknowledge and thank emergency services and police for responding so quickly, and their ongoing work in treating the injured.

“Rugby league brings people together, and this should have been a weekend of excitement and pride for Newcastle fans.”

Multiple fundraisers were launched on Saturday afternoon by friends and loved ones of injured fans, including for a five-year-old child who was placed in an induced coma after suffering serious injuries.

The child has already required multiple operations, according to organiser Ashleigh Gibbs.

“Their mum was also seriously injured and will require multiple operations and a long period of recovery,” the fundraising page says.

“Both mum and child now have a long road ahead of them, with ongoing surgeries, hospital stays, rehabilitation.”

- Australian Associated Press contributed to this report

australia.title: Is now a good time to switch banks for a better home loan rate? Here’s what to know after the latest RBA hike
australia.snippet: Experts warn it’s getting harder to find big discounts and borrowers will need to talk tough about leaving their mortgage lender for anot...
australia.content:
Mortgage holders may save hundreds of dollars a month by switching banks now that the lowest interest rates are close to 6%, after the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted its key rate to the highest level in 15 years.

But professionals warn it’s getting harder to find big discounts.

Here’s what you need to know about getting a better rate.

Lowest rates are near 6%

The average variable mortgage rate for owner-occupiers will be 6.49% once Tuesday’s rate increase is passed on, Reserve Bank data shows.

But some banks are offering rates close to 6%. Switching from the average rate to that lower rate would represent a $180 cut to monthly repayments, for someone with a $600,000 loan with 25 years left in their term.

Among the big four banks, Westpac is offering the lowest variable rate at 6.24%, according to comparison platform Canstar. Dozens of smaller lenders are offering lower rates than the big four.

Canstar data indicates just two lenders will offer variable rates under 6% once Tuesday’s rate increase is passed on.

If the RBA hikes interest rates again, the lowest variable rate will likely lift to 6.25%.

A handful of lenders, typically smaller banks and credit unions, are offering fixed rates below 6%, mostly hovering at 5.99%. The fixed rates on offer have risen in recent months as markets grow more certain the RBA’s next move will be another hike, not a cut.

Record refinancing

Borrowers can sometimes get a better rate just by calling up their own bank and seeking a rate review, though it’s often more difficult to get a real discount.

Sally Tindall, Canstar’s director of data insights, says borrowers have a better chance of convincing their bank if they talk tough about leaving for another lender.

Tindall says borrowers should call once they know their own rate, their lender’s best rate and better rates across the sector – or better yet, have an offer from another bank.

“If you really want to put your best haggling foot forward, get yourself prepared, with … a competitor offer, and be prepared to ask for a mortgage discharge form,” Tindall says.

Switching lenders can take over a month and typically costs more than $1,000 but the one-time fees may be offset by the longer-term benefits of a lower rate.

Plenty of Australians are switching their home loans, with a record $65bn worth of external refinancing in the first half of 2026, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics data. Credit agencies say refinancing applications have held up since June.

But falling house prices mean a growing number of Australians will be locked out from refinancing because they don’t have adequate borrowing capacity.

The share of Australians with loan to value ratios (LVRs) of more than 80% has risen this year, with recent buyers especially likely to have seen their values slip, according to the Reserve Bank.

The chief executive of broking group Aussie, Sebastian Watkins, says borrowers with LVRs above 80% are in “mortgage prison” and are less likely to be offered a lower rate.

“As values fall, loan-to-value rates rise [and] once you push above 80%, the door to a competitive refinance can start to slam shut,” Watkins says.

Rebecca Jarrett-Dalton, a Sydney mortgage broker, says banks have become less willing to offer better rates.

Waiting before switching

More than 40 lenders have announced new rates since the RBA decision, Canstar says.

But many lenders will wait to publicly announce and others will avoid publicising their decision entirely.

Jarrett-Dalton says that makes it difficult to judge the best ongoing rate in the days after a cash rate increase.

Borrowers who wait a few weeks will have a better chance of seeing whether a rate that seemed too good to be true will lift after the hike or still run at a discount.

On the upside, with September over, workers will have three months’ worth of pay records for the financial year that started in July.

Jarrett-Dalton says lenders will now be able to account for regular additional income they might otherwise have ignored in applications, such as overtime, weekend loading or allowances.

world.title: Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities
world.snippet: Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down Allegations that the son of the Liby...
world.content:
Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.

Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.

But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.

Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.

Donald Trump’s Africa adviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.

Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”

But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.

Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.

On 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.

Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.

The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.

Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”

He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.

The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.

Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.

world.title: Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin
world.snippet: Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric cla...
world.content:
On the eve of the Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.

Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by a group of young volunteers, Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.

But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the 14th-century BCE pharaoh’s origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.

Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.

The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.

Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.

“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.

“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”

Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.

One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.

Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.

“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.

“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.

This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.

Monica Hanna, a prominent Egyptologist and assistant professor of archaeology at the American University of Iraq–Baghdad, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.

“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”

Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.

They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.

“That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.

Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.

“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.

  • This article is published in collaboration with Egab

world.title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad
world.snippet: Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights With hours left befor...
world.content:
With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.

On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.

Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF).

Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa.

“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”

The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, immigration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.

“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.

“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”

A Democratic congressional aide said Shaheen had maintained 10 holds on $22m of awards focusing on Brazil, South Africa, Nigeria, and the promotion of a rightwing ideology in the United Kingdom and in Europe. According to the aide, secretary of state Marco Rubio had personally signed a memo to disregard the holds and obligate the funds.

The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.

In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).

Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.

The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”.

“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe, which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse.

The Guardian first reported that Trump officials had drawn up no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe. ProPublica similarly reported that there were at least a dozen no-bid grants earmarked for rightwing projects.

The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.

A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.

A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.

One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.

And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.

The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and enforced by Ofcom, it has age-verification rules – which took effect last year – that have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.

The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.

The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, regarding issues including online safety law to immigration.

world.title: South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings
world.snippet: President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women South Africa’s president has called on men to take mo...
world.content:
South Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders.

Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.

In a televised speech on Tuesday night, the president said local governments would have five months to address issues that compromised women’s safety, from broken streetlights to overgrown public spaces and abandoned buildings. He added that he had tasked five ministers to come up with a plan within 60 days to reduce alcohol-fuelled violence.

“Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” Ramaphosa said. “But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort.

“Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence or enforce a law.”

South Africa has been gripped by grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Eight of the women were found in the last three weeks, including Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who was discovered on 12 September after she went missing when she went for a run after work.

Ramaphosa said suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings and that the other cases would not be left to go cold. He added that police had not found evidence that a serial killer was responsible for all 11 killings, but that all possibilities were still being investigated.

He directly addressed South African men, urging them to challenge relatives, friends and colleagues who harassed, humiliated or abused women. “It is time for good men to stop being silent men,” he said.

“For too long, gender-based violence has been treated as a woman’s problem to solve. Women march, the women of our country organise, they speak out, they protest, they confront and they comfort survivors,” Ramaphosa said.

“Women change their routes home. Avoid going out at night and warn one another about dangerous places and dangerous men. We have placed the burden of male violence on women. That must change.”

Activists expressed their frustration that solid policy actions had not been taken years ago and scepticism that the measures Ramaphosa had announced would work.

Shenilla Mohamed, the executive director of Amnesty International South Africa, said: “These are not new issues and as a country we have been talking about ways to tackle the high numbers of [gender-based violence and femicide], especially since 2019 when women took to the streets to protest, and yet here we are again in the face of continued attacks against women.

“Amnesty International South Africa also notes the timelines put in place by the president, but this will only mean something if it results in action, and if there are consequences for inaction.”

Mpiwa Mangwiro-Tsanga and Bafana Khumalo, of Sonke Gender Justice, an NGO, said: “Our concern … is that the response remains heavily weighted towards what happens after violence has already occurred.”

They added: “Investigating unresolved cases, processing forensic evidence and repairing unsafe public spaces are necessary, but they do not constitute a comprehensive prevention strategy. It is concerning that the president is asking municipalities to do what is actually their mandate and yet they do not deliver on these.”

world.title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US
world.snippet: Burundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policy Burundi has agreed to join a clutc...
world.content:
Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under ⁠Donald Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration ​policy.

However, Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said ⁠Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial ⁠details.

Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to about half ​a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals ‌that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of ‌dollars.

In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.

Mutoni said preparations were under way to arrange accommodation, ‌living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they ​will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.

“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law ⁠will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.

Burundi aimed ​to both ​strengthen diplomatic relations and provide ​hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson ​added.

The US ‌state department ​did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.
